questions.q: Squeezing a lemon between your fingers is an example of a force doing which of these?
o: Changing the shape of an object
Changing the direction of a moving object
Setting an object at rest into motion
Bringing a moving object to rest
questions.a: Changing the shape of an object: the fingers press the lemon out of shape.

questions.q: The north pole of one bar magnet is brought close to the north pole of another. Which description of the magnetic force between them is correct?
o: The magnets repel each other, pushing apart
The magnets attract each other, pulling together
There is no force until the magnets touch
They attract each other only if the magnets are large
questions.a: Like poles repel, so the two magnets push each other apart.

questions.q: Ritu hangs her school bag from a spring balance and the scale reads 40 N. What does this reading tell her?
o: The Earth pulls the bag downward with a force of magnitude 40 N
The mass of the bag is 40 N
The spring pushes the bag downward with 40 N
questions.a: The reading is the weight of the bag: the Earth's gravitational pull on it, of magnitude 40 N, acting downward. Newton is a unit of force, not of mass.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about force.
I. Like velocity, force is a quantity for which a direction must be stated along with its magnitude and unit.
II. The weight of an object is the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls it.
III. The full name of the unit of force is written with a capital letter, as 'Newton'.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: the unit is written 'newton' with a small n; only its symbol N is a capital.

questions.q: State the SI unit of force and its symbol. What does the magnitude of a force express?
questions.a: The SI unit of force is the newton, symbol N. The magnitude of a force expresses its strength.
s: Names the newton as the unit and N as its symbol
States that the magnitude expresses the strength of the force

questions.q: True or False: 'A spring balance can measure only the weight of an object.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. A spring balance measures the magnitude of a force in general: if you pull its free end, it measures the force with which you pull the spring inside it.
s: Reason: it measures any pulling force, e.g. the pull on its free end, not only weight

questions.q: Give the direction of each force. (a) The force of friction on a box that is being pushed towards the left along the floor. (b) The gravitational force of the Earth on a mango hanging from a tree. (c) The electrostatic force between two balloons that carry like charges.
questions.a: (a) Towards the right, opposite to the motion. (b) Downward, towards the Earth. (c) The balloons repel, so each is pushed away from the other.
s: (a) friction acts to the right, opposite to the motion
(b) the Earth's pull is downward, towards the Earth
(c) like charges repel, pushing the balloons apart

questions.q: A worker in a warehouse pulls a goods trolley with a rope tied to a spring balance. The balance reads 22 N while he pulls towards the north. (a) Name two quantities from the study of motion that, like force, need a direction. (b) What three things together describe a force completely? (c) A classmate writes only '22 N' for this pull. Why is it not a complete description? (d) Write the complete description of the pull.
questions.a: (a) Any two of position, displacement, velocity and acceleration. (b) Its magnitude, its unit and its direction. (c) '22 N' gives only the magnitude (the strength) of the force, not its direction; a change in direction changes the effect. (d) 22 N towards the north.
s: (a) two of position, displacement, velocity, acceleration
(c) '22 N' gives only the magnitude; the direction is missing and it changes the effect

questions.q: Two forces act on a book lying on a table: 8 N towards the right and 3 N towards the left. What is the net force on the book?
questions.a: 5 N towards the right: the forces are opposite, so the net force is the difference, 8 N - 3 N = 5 N, in the direction of the larger force.

questions.q: Two forces acting on an object are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. What are such forces called?
questions.a: Balanced forces: their net force is zero.

questions.q:
Match column I with column II.
Column I: 1. Balanced forces  2. Unbalanced forces  3. Net force of two forces in the same direction  4. Net force of two unequal forces in opposite directions
Column II: P. Zero net force  Q. A non-zero net force  R. Sum of the two magnitudes  S. Difference of the two magnitudes
questions.a: 1-P, 2-Q, 3-R, 4-S: balanced forces give zero net force, unbalanced forces a non-zero one; forces in the same direction add, unequal opposite forces subtract.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A book lying on a table stays at rest even though forces act on it.
Reason (R): The weight of the book is balanced by the normal force from the table, so the net force on it is zero.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the downward weight and the upward normal force are equal and opposite, so they are balanced, the net force is zero and the book stays at rest.

questions.q: Two forces of 15 N and 9 N act on a crate along one straight line. Find the net force (magnitude and direction) when (a) both act towards the east, (b) the 15 N force acts towards the east and the 9 N force acts towards the west.
questions.a: (a) 15 N + 9 N = 24 N towards the east. (b) 15 N - 9 N = 6 N towards the east.

questions.q: True or False: 'An object can have more than one force acting on it and still have zero net force.' Give the verdict and an example.
questions.a: True. A ball floating on water has the Earth's gravitational force acting downward and the buoyant force acting upward; they balance, so the net force is zero. The motion depends only on the net force.
s: Example with two balanced forces, e.g. a floating ball (gravitational down, buoyant up)

questions.q: In a tug of war the rope moves slowly towards team B. The captain of team A says, 'We pulled with 450 N, so team B must have pulled with less than 450 N.' Is the captain right? Explain using net force.
questions.a: No. A rope moves in the direction of the larger force, so team B pulled with more than 450 N. The net force is (B's pull - 450 N), acting towards team B.
s: Verdict: No, the captain is wrong
The rope moves in the direction of the larger force
So B pulled with more than 450 N; net force = B's pull - 450 N, towards B

questions.q: In a furniture shop three workers move a sofa along a straight line. Ali pushes it with 120 N towards the east, Bina pushes it with 90 N towards the east and Chetan pulls it with 150 N towards the west. Consider only these three forces. (a) Find the net force of Ali's and Bina's pushes. (b) Find the net force when Chetan's pull is included. (c) In which direction does the sofa move? (d) What pull must Chetan apply instead to make the forces balanced? (e) Bina stops pushing while Ali and Chetan carry on as before. Find the new net force.
questions.a: (a) 120 + 90 = 210 N towards the east. (b) 210 - 150 = 60 N towards the east. (c) Towards the east, the direction of the net force. (d) 210 N towards the west. (e) 150 - 120 = 30 N towards the west.
s: (c) the sofa moves towards the east
(d) Chetan must pull with 210 N towards the west

questions.q: At a village fair in Mysuru, Team Green has four members who pull a rope with 150 N, 140 N, 135 N and 125 N. Team Yellow has five members who pull the other way with 120 N, 115 N, 110 N, 105 N and 100 N. All pulls act along the rope. (a) Find the total pull of Team Green. (b) Find the total pull of Team Yellow. (c) Find the net force on the rope and say whether the rope moves. (d) Yellow's captain wants the team to win by a net force of 20 N, with every member pulling the same amount harder. How much harder must each Yellow member pull?
questions.a: (a) 150 + 140 + 135 + 125 = 550 N. (b) 120 + 115 + 110 + 105 + 100 = 550 N. (c) 550 - 550 = 0 N; the forces are balanced and the rope does not move. (d) Yellow needs a total pull of 550 + 20 = 570 N, that is 20 N more shared by five members, so each must pull 20/5 = 4 N harder.
s: (c) net force zero, balanced, rope does not move
(d) 20 N extra over 5 members: 4 N harder each

questions.q: In which direction does the force of friction act on an object sliding along a floor?
o: Opposite to the direction of its motion
In the direction of its motion
questions.a: Opposite to the direction of its motion.

questions.q: A box rests on a floor. What is the name of the upward force that the floor exerts on the box, perpendicular to the surface?
questions.a: The normal force: it acts upward, perpendicular to the surface, and balances the weight.

questions.q: A block is pulled with a spring balance on four carrom boards, and the reading when it just starts to move is: board P 3.5 N, board Q 7 N, board R 5 N, board S 4 N. A coin is then flicked with the same push on each board. On which board will it slide the farthest?
questions.a: Board P: its reading (3.5 N) is the smallest, so its friction is the smallest, the velocity falls most slowly and the coin travels the largest distance.

questions.q:
A stack of coins is pushed back against a stretched rubber band and released. Consider the following statements.
I. Before release, the forces on the stack are balanced.
II. After the stack loses contact with the rubber band, the band's force continues to push it forward.
III. On a smoother surface, the velocity of the stack decreases more slowly.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: once contact is lost the rubber band's force no longer acts; only friction acts, opposite to the motion.

questions.q: A box is being pushed along a level floor. Name the four forces acting on it and give the direction of each.
questions.a: Applied force (forward) and force of friction (backward, opposite to the motion); weight or gravitational force (downward) and normal force (upward, perpendicular to the floor).
s: Applied force forward and friction backward
Weight downward and normal force upward

questions.q: Gauri pushes a heavy almirah gently and it does not move. She says, 'No friction is acting, because nothing is moving.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. Friction acts on the almirah opposite to her push and balances it, so the net force is zero and the almirah stays at rest. It will move only when her push becomes larger than the force of friction.
s: Friction acts opposite to her push and balances it (net force zero)
It moves only when the push is larger than the friction

questions.q: A shopkeeper drags the same sack of rice with a spring balance across four floors. The reading when the sack just starts to move is: marble 12 N, tiled 15 N, wooden 20 N, cemented 26 N. (a) On which floor is the friction the largest? (b) On which floor is it the smallest? (c) He drags the sack towards the shop door. In which direction does friction act on it? (d) On the cemented floor he first pulls with 20 N. Does the sack move? Why? (e) He then pulls with 30 N on the cemented floor. Taking the friction as 26 N, find the net force on the sack.
questions.a: (a) Cemented floor (26 N). (b) Marble floor (12 N). (c) Away from the door, opposite to the motion. (d) No: 20 N is smaller than the largest friction (26 N) the floor can offer, so friction matches the pull (20 N), the net force is zero and the sack stays at rest. (e) 30 N - 26 N = 4 N towards the door.
s: (c) away from the door, opposite to the motion
(d) no, 20 N is less than the largest friction of 26 N, so friction matches the pull

questions.q: For a science fair in Lucknow, students launch the same toy cart with the same stretch of a rubber band on three tracks. After leaving the band, the cart travels 1.2 m on track A, 2.0 m on track B and 0.8 m on track C before stopping. (a) On which track is the friction largest? (b) Why does the cart slow down after leaving the rubber band? (c) Arrange the tracks in increasing order of the spring-balance reading needed to just start a block moving on them. (d) The organisers want a long racing lane followed by a short stopping zone where the carts must halt quickly. Which track should be used for each? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Track C, where the cart travels the least. (b) Only friction acts on it, opposite to its motion, so its velocity decreases until it stops. (c) B, A, C (smallest friction to largest). (d) Use track B for the racing lane, because its friction is smallest and the cart keeps its speed longest; use track C for the stopping zone, because its larger friction brings the cart to rest in the shortest distance.
s: (b) friction alone acts opposite to the motion and reduces the velocity
(d) B for racing (least friction), C for stopping (most friction), with reason

questions.q: Which word did Newton use for the tendency of objects to resist a change in their state of rest or uniform motion?
questions.a: Inertia.

questions.q: In Newton's first law, what does it mean when an object is said to be 'at rest'?
o: Its acceleration is constant but not zero
A net force is acting on it
Its position changes at a steady rate
questions.a: Its velocity is zero.

questions.q: A lift in a mall moves upward at a steady 2 m/s in a straight line. What is the net force on the lift?
o: Upward, because the lift is moving up
Equal to the weight of the lift, upward
questions.a: Zero: its velocity is constant, so its acceleration is zero and by the first law no net force acts on it.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A ball rolling on a level floor slows down and finally stops.
Reason (R): If the net force acting on an object is zero, its acceleration is zero.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the ball stops because friction acts on it opposite to its motion, so the net force on it is not zero.

questions.q: A cyclist rides due north at a constant velocity of 4 m/s, with zero net force on her bicycle. (a) What is her velocity after 30 s? (b) How far does she travel in those 30 s?
questions.a: (a) Still 4 m/s due north, since with zero net force the velocity does not change. (b) 4 m/s x 30 s = 120 m, towards the north.

questions.q: A puck slides on almost frictionless ice at 3 m/s. Ravi says, 'Nothing is pushing the puck forward, so it must be slowing down.' True or False? Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. With almost no friction the net force on the puck is (nearly) zero, so by the first law it continues moving with a constant velocity of 3 m/s; no force is needed to keep a moving object moving, only to change its velocity.
s: Reason: net force about zero, so by the first law its velocity stays constant; a force is needed only to change velocity

questions.q: No net force acts on an object. Describe (a) its position-time graph if it is at rest, (b) its velocity-time graph if it is at rest, (c) its velocity-time graph if it is moving with a constant velocity.
questions.a: (a) A straight line parallel to the time axis: the position does not change. (b) The velocity stays zero, so the line lies along the time axis. (c) A straight line parallel to the time axis at the value of the constant velocity.
s: (b) velocity zero all the time, line along the time axis
(c) horizontal line at the constant velocity

questions.q: Use Newton's first law of motion to answer the following. (a) A camera drone hovers at rest in still air. Its weight is 15 N downward. What upward force must its propellers give it, and why? (b) A crane lowers a crate straight down at a constant velocity of 0.5 m/s. Ignoring air, the crate's weight is 800 N. What upward pull does the rope give the crate? (c) The rope's pull on the crate in (b) suddenly falls to 750 N. Will the crate keep its constant velocity? Why? (d) A bus moving at a constant velocity brakes suddenly, and a book lying on its smooth seat slides forward. Explain why, using the first law.
questions.a: (a) 15 N upward: the drone is at rest, so the net force on it is zero and the upward force must balance its weight. (b) 800 N upward: at constant velocity the net force is zero, so the rope's pull equals the weight. (c) No: the net force becomes 800 N - 750 N = 50 N downward, a non-zero net force, so the velocity of the crate changes (it speeds up downward). (d) The brakes act on the bus, not on the book; with almost no net force on it, the book continues moving forward with its earlier velocity while the bus slows down, so it slides forward on the seat.
s: (a) 15 N upward, since zero net force is needed to stay at rest
(b) 800 N upward, since constant velocity means zero net force
(c) no: net force 50 N downward, so the velocity changes
(d) almost no net force acts on the book, so it keeps its velocity while the bus slows

questions.q: A trolley moves along a straight corridor. Its velocity is recorded every second: at 0 s, 1 s, 2 s, 3 s, 4 s, 5 s and 6 s it is 0, 2, 4, 4, 4, 2 and 0 m/s. (a) In which time interval is the net force on the trolley zero? Give the reason. (b) In which intervals does a net force act, and in which direction in each? (c) Describe its position-time graph from 2 s to 4 s. (d) Find the distance it covers from 2 s to 4 s. (e) Rahul says, 'From 2 s to 4 s nobody needs to push the trolley, because it is already moving.' The corridor floor has friction. Is he right?
questions.a: (a) 2 s to 4 s: the velocity stays at 4 m/s, so the acceleration and the net force are zero. (b) 0 s to 2 s, forward (velocity increasing); 4 s to 6 s, backward (velocity decreasing). (c) A straight line inclined to the time axis, since the trolley covers equal distances in equal times. (d) 4 m/s x 2 s = 8 m. (e) No: on a floor with friction, someone must keep pushing with a force equal to the friction so that the net force stays zero; without the push, friction would slow it down. Only on a frictionless floor would no push be needed.
s: (a) 2-4 s, velocity constant so net force zero
(e) No: a push equal to friction is needed to keep the net force zero

questions.q: A net force of 15 N acts on a box of mass 3 kg. What is the acceleration of the box?
questions.a: 5 m/s2, since a = F/m = 15 N / 3 kg.

questions.q: One newton is the force that produces an acceleration of 1 m/s2 on an object of mass
questions.a: 1 kg.

questions.q: Using g = 9.8 m/s2, what is the weight of a suitcase of mass 12 kg?
questions.a: 117.6 N, since F = mg = 12 kg x 9.8 m/s2.

questions.q:
Match each situation in column I with the reason in column II.
Column I: 1. A fielder draws his hands back while catching a fast ball  2. A 2 kg stone and a 7 kg stone dropped together reach the ground together  3. A coconut thrown down on hard ground cracks  4. The mass of a cart is doubled for the same pull
Column II: P. The stopping time is made longer, so a smaller force acts  Q. The larger gravitational force acts on a proportionally larger mass, so the acceleration is the same  R. The velocity falls to zero in a very short time, so a very large force acts  S. The same force gives half the acceleration
State Newton's second law of motion and write it as an equation.
questions.a: When a net force acts on an object, it accelerates in the direction of the net force; the acceleration is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass. F = ma (or a = F/m).
s: Statement: acceleration in the direction of the net force, proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass
Equation F = ma or a = F/m

questions.q: A net force of 12 N acts on a 2 kg trolley and, separately, on a 4 kg trolley. True or False: 'The 4 kg trolley gets twice the acceleration of the 2 kg trolley.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. a = F/m gives 12/2 = 6 m/s2 for the 2 kg trolley and 12/4 = 3 m/s2 for the 4 kg trolley, so the 4 kg trolley gets half the acceleration: for a fixed force the acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass.
s: Reason: 6 m/s2 and 3 m/s2, so doubling the mass halves the acceleration

questions.q: A crate of mass 50 kg rests on a level floor. The largest force of friction the floor can offer is 70 N, and a worker pushes it with a constant 95 N. (a) Find the net force on the crate. (b) Find its acceleration. (c) Find how far it moves in the first 4 s, starting from rest.

An e-rickshaw with its load has a mass of 600 kg and moves towards the east. Its velocity rises steadily from 0 to 6 m/s in the first 4 s, stays at 6 m/s from 4 s to 10 s, and falls steadily to 0 from 10 s to 13 s. (a) Find its acceleration from 0 s to 4 s. (b) Find the net force on it from 0 s to 4 s. (c) What is the net force from 4 s to 10 s? Why? (d) Find the net force from 10 s to 13 s, with its direction. (e) In which interval is the magnitude of the net force larger, 0-4 s or 10-13 s, and why?
questions.a: (a) a = (6 - 0)/4 = 1.5 m/s2. (b) F = 600 x 1.5 = 900 N towards the east. (c) Zero, because the velocity is constant. (d) a = (0 - 6)/3 = -2 m/s2, so F = 600 x (-2) = -1200 N, that is 1200 N towards the west. (e) 10-13 s: the same change in velocity (6 m/s) happens in a shorter time, so the acceleration and the force are larger.
s: (e) 10-13 s, same velocity change in less time

questions.q: A Class 9 group in Bhopal pulls a cart along a table with a thread and records three trials. Trial 1: cart of 2 kg, pull of the thread 1 N. Trial 2: the same 2 kg cart, pull of the thread 2 N. Trial 3: a cart of 4 kg, pull of the thread 2 N. Ignoring friction, (a) find the acceleration in trial 1. (b) Find the acceleration in trial 2 and say what doubling the force did. (c) Find the acceleration in trial 3 and compare it with trial 2. (d) In trial 2 the group actually measured 0.9 m/s2 and one member says Newton's second law is wrong. Do you agree? Justify.
questions.a: (a) a = 1/2 = 0.5 m/s2. (b) a = 2/2 = 1 m/s2; doubling the force doubled the acceleration. (c) a = 2/4 = 0.5 m/s2, half of trial 2: doubling the mass halved the acceleration. (d) No: the friction between the cart's wheels and the table makes the net force a little less than the pull of the thread, and there are measurement errors, so a value a little less than 1 m/s2 is expected; it is not a failure of the law.
s: (d) disagree: friction of the wheels and measurement errors explain the lower value

questions.q: According to Newton's third law, the two forces of an action-reaction pair act on
o: only objects that touch each other
questions.a: Two different objects, which is why the pair never balances.

questions.q: When a person walks, which force actually pushes her forward?
o: The force of friction from the ground on her foot
The push of her foot on the ground, backward
The gravitational force of the Earth on her
The normal force of the ground on her
questions.a: The force of friction from the ground on her foot, acting forward, in reply to her foot pushing the ground backward.

questions.q: An inflated balloon is taped to a straw on a taut thread. Its neck is opened and air rushes out towards the left. In which direction does the balloon move?
o: Up and down along the thread
questions.a: Towards the right: the air rushing out pushes the balloon with an equal force in the opposite direction.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. The Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 slowed down by firing its engine in the direction of its motion.
II. A rocket lifts off because the upward force of the exhaust gas on it is larger than its weight.
III. Two similarly charged balloons exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III: all three are correct. Newton's third law applies to non-contact forces such as electrostatic forces too.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A rocket can lift off from its launch pad.
Reason (R): The two forces of a Newton's third law pair act on the same object and balance each other.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the two forces of a third-law pair act on different objects (the gas and the rocket), so they do not balance each other.

questions.q: On a still lake, Ramesh sits in a boat (boat and Ramesh together 200 kg) and pulls a rope tied to an empty boat of 100 kg with a force of 50 N. Ignore the drag of the water. (a) What force acts on Ramesh's boat, and in which direction? (b) Find the initial accelerations of the two boats.
questions.a: (a) 50 N, towards the empty boat (equal and opposite to his pull). (b) Ramesh's boat: 50/200 = 0.25 m/s2; empty boat: 50/100 = 0.5 m/s2.
s: (a) 50 N on his boat, towards the empty boat

questions.q: In each case, name the force that the second object exerts on the first, with its direction. (a) A boy's foot kicks a football forward. (b) Sitting on a wheeled chair with her feet off the floor, a girl pushes a heavy table forward with her hands. (c) Sitting on a bicycle without pedalling, a rider pushes the ground backward with her feet.
questions.a: (a) The ball pushes the foot backward with an equal force. (b) The table pushes the girl backward with an equal force, so she and the chair move backward. (c) The ground pushes her feet forward with an equal force (friction), so she moves forward with the bicycle.

questions.q: Magnet A (0.3 kg) and magnet B (0.1 kg) lie on a smooth table and attract each other. A pulls B with a force of 0.6 N. Asha says, 'A is the bigger magnet, so B pulls A with a smaller force, and that is why A moves less.' Check her claim.
questions.a: She is right that A moves less but wrong about the reason. By the third law B pulls A with an equal 0.6 N, even for non-contact magnetic forces. A's acceleration is 0.6/0.3 = 2 m/s2 and B's is 0.6/0.1 = 6 m/s2, so A accelerates less because its mass is larger, not because the force on it is smaller.
s: B pulls A with an equal 0.6 N (third law applies to magnetic forces)
Verdict: right that A moves less, wrong about the reason: larger mass, not a smaller force

questions.q: At a heritage show in a fort, a display cannon of mass 800 kg stands on smooth wheels. When it is fired, the cannon pushes a cannonball of mass 8 kg forward with a force of 4000 N. (a) What force acts on the cannon during firing, and in which direction? (b) Find the initial acceleration of the cannonball. (c) Find the initial acceleration of the cannon. (d) The organisers want the cannon's recoil acceleration to be less than 3 m/s2. Plan X: fix the cannon on a 600 kg stone-loaded carriage that moves with it. Plan Y: fire a lighter 5 kg ball with the same force of 4000 N. Which plan works? Show with numbers.
questions.a: (a) 4000 N backward, by Newton's third law. (b) 4000/8 = 500 m/s2. (c) 4000/800 = 5 m/s2. (d) Plan X: the recoil force 4000 N now acts on 800 + 600 = 1400 kg, so a = 4000/1400 = 2.9 m/s2 (about), less than 3 m/s2, so it works. Plan Y: the force on the cannon is still 4000 N on 800 kg, so a = 5 m/s2; a lighter ball does not reduce the recoil force, so it fails. Plan X works.
s: (d) Plan X: 4000/1400 = 2.9 m/s2 < 3; Plan Y still 5 m/s2, so Plan X

questions.q: Boxes of 2 kg and 8 kg are joined by a string on a frictionless floor, and a horizontal force of 20 N pulls the 2 kg box. What is the acceleration of the system?
questions.a: 2 m/s2, since a = F/(m1 + m2) = 20 N / 10 kg.

questions.q: Two boxes joined by a string are treated as one system and pulled by a force F. What kind of force is the tension in the string?
questions.a: An internal force: it acts within the system and need not be considered to find the system's acceleration.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): For two boxes of masses m1 and m2 joined by a string on a frictionless surface, a force F pulling box 1 gives the system an acceleration of F/m1.
Reason (R): When the two boxes and the string are treated as one system, the tension in the string is an internal force and need not be considered.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: the system accelerates like a single object of mass m1 + m2, so a = F/(m1 + m2).

questions.q: Boxes of 7 kg and 3 kg are joined by a string on a frictionless surface and pulled by a horizontal force of 25 N. (a) What is the mass of the system? (b) Find its acceleration.
True or False: 'For two boxes joined by a string on a horizontal surface, the combined weight of the boxes is balanced by the combined normal force from the ground.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The gravitational force (m1 + m2)g acts downward on the system and the normal force (N1 + N2) acts upward; these external vertical forces balance, so only the pull F gives the acceleration.
s: Reason: (m1 + m2)g downward balanced by (N1 + N2) upward

questions.q: Two toy trolleys of 1.2 kg and 1.8 kg are joined by a thread on a frictionless floor and pulled with a horizontal force of 6 N. Take g = 9.8 m/s2. (a) Find the acceleration of the system. (b) Find the combined weight of the trolleys. (c) What is the combined normal force from the floor, and in which direction does it act?
questions.a: (a) a = 6 N / 3 kg = 2 m/s2. (b) (1.2 + 1.8) x 9.8 = 29.4 N, downward. (c) 29.4 N, upward, balancing the combined weight.

questions.q: Meera must pull two boxes of 6 kg and 10 kg, joined by a string on a frictionless floor, so that they reach an acceleration of 1.5 m/s2. She can pull with at most 20 N. (a) Find the mass of the system. (b) Find the acceleration her 20 N pull gives. (c) Find the force needed for 1.5 m/s2. (d) She may unhook one box and pull only the other. Which box should she keep so that her 20 N still gives at least 1.5 m/s2 while moving as much mass as possible? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 6 + 10 = 16 kg. (b) 20/16 = 1.25 m/s2, which is too small. (c) F = 16 x 1.5 = 24 N, more than she can pull. (d) Keep the 10 kg box: 20/10 = 2 m/s2, which is at least 1.5 m/s2, and it is the larger mass (keeping the 6 kg box also works, 20/6 = 3.33 m/s2, but moves less mass).
s: (d) keep the 10 kg box: 2 m/s2 meets the target with the larger mass

questions.q: At a railway parcel office in Vijayawada, two parcel carts are joined by a short chain on a smooth floor where friction can be neglected. Cart A has a mass of 30 kg and cart B a mass of 20 kg. A porter pulls cart A forward with a horizontal force of 100 N. (a) Find the mass of the system of two carts. (b) Find the acceleration of the system. (c) Name the internal force in the chain. (d) A 50 kg parcel is loaded onto cart B and the pull stays 100 N. Find the new acceleration.
questions.a: (a) 30 + 20 = 50 kg. (b) a = 100 N / 50 kg = 2 m/s2. (c) The tension in the chain. (d) 100 N / 100 kg = 1 m/s2, half of the earlier value.
